title: Water shortages in a rainy country

turns.speaker: Asha
turns.text: Hosepipe ban again, in a region that had above-average rainfall last winter. That's the bit I can't square.

turns.speaker: Milo
turns.text: Rainfall isn't the constraint. Storage is, and we haven't built a major reservoir in about thirty years.

turns.speaker: Fintan
turns.text: And the leaks. Something like a fifth of treated water never reaches a tap.

turns.speaker: Fintan
turns.text: Roughly, and it's been roughly that for a long time. Fixing the last of it costs more than it saves, which is the honest reason it persists.

turns.speaker: Milo
turns.text: Except the comparison should be against building a reservoir, not against nothing. Leaks are the cheapest water there is.

turns.speaker: Asha
turns.text: Household use gets all the attention and it's about a fifth of the total. Agriculture and industry are the rest.

turns.speaker: Asha
turns.text: So we're told to take shorter showers while a field of thirsty crops is irrigated in August.

turns.speaker: Milo
turns.text: Metering does shift household use, to be fair. About a tenth, consistently.

turns.speaker: Fintan
turns.text: And it hits large families hardest, which is the objection that stopped it here.

turns.speaker: Asha
turns.text: You can price the first block low and the rest higher. That's solvable.

turns.speaker: Milo
turns.text: It is. It's just less popular than telling people to take shorter showers.

points: Hosepipe bans follow a winter of above-average rainfall, indicating storage rather than rainfall is the constraint.
No major reservoir has been built in about thirty years.
Roughly a fifth of treated water is lost to leaks, justified on cost grounds, though Milo argues the comparison should be against building new storage.
Household use is about a fifth of total consumption, with agriculture and industry accounting for the rest.
Metering reduces household use by around a tenth but is objected to as unfair on large families.
Asha notes tiered pricing solves that objection, though it is less politically appealing than asking for shorter showers.
